questions.subject: network-theory
questions.question: In the following circuit, i(t) under steady state is
questions.explanation:
To analyze the network containing multiple electrical excitation frequencies, we apply the superposition theorem. This allows us to compute the individual steady-state response contributions by considering one source active at a time. 1: Response due to the \(5\,\text{V}\) DC source For a pure DC excitation, the angular frequency component is: \[\omega = 0\,\text{rad/s}\] Since inductive reactance \(X_{L} \propto \omega\) and capacitive reactance \(X_{c} \propto \frac{1}{\omega}\), at zero frequency: a. The inductor behaves as an ideal short circuit (\(X_{L} = 0\,\Omega\)). b. The capacitor behaves as an ideal open circuit (\(X_{c} \rightarrow \infty\,\Omega\)). Consequently, no alternating or direct continuous loop current flows through this reactive series path due to the isolating break introduced by the capacitor: \[i_{1}(t) = 0\,\text{A}\] 2: Response due to the \(10 \sin t\) AC voltage source For this harmonic source configuration, the operating frequency parameter is: \[\omega = 1\,\text{rad/s}\] The individual branch reactive elements are converted to their respective frequency-domain expressions: \[X_{L} = j\omega L = j2\,\Omega\] \[X_{c} = \frac{-j}{\omega C} = \frac{-j}{(1)(1)} = -j\,\Omega\] The total series input impedance \(Z\) presentation encountered by the AC source is: \[Z = 1 + j2 - j = 1 + j1\,\Omega = \sqrt{2} \angle 45^{\circ}\,\Omega\] Expressing the AC input voltage source excitation in phasor form using sine phase tracking: \[\vec{V} = 10 \angle 0^{\circ}\,\text{V}\] The current phasor \(\vec{I}\) driven through the loop is calculated via Ohm's law: \[\vec{I} = \frac{\vec{V}}{Z} = \frac{10 \angle 0^{\circ}}{\sqrt{2} \angle 45^{\circ}} = 7.07 \angle -45^{\circ}\,\text{A}\] Transforming this phasor back into its corresponding time-domain formulation yields: \[i_{2}(t) = 7.07 \sin(t - 45^{\circ})\,\text{A}\] The net time-varying current profile \(i(t)\) is the algebraic sum of the separate contributions: \[i(t) = i_{1}(t) + i_{2}(t) = 0 + 7.07 \sin(t - 45^{\circ})\,\text{A}\] \[i(t) = 7.07 \sin(t - 45^{\circ})\,\text{A}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Never compute a combined equivalent impedance by mixing or adding different operational frequencies (\(\omega\)) directly.
  • Ensure that the time-domain reference phase matches the initial function profile (\(\sin t\)) used during the polar phasor mapping stage.
\[\boxed{(d) 7.07 \sin (t-45^{\circ})}\]

questions.subject: network-theory
questions.question: The following circuit (figure) resonates at
questions.explanation: The expression for the equivalent input impedance \(Z\) of the given network is: \[Z = 10 + \left( j4\omega - \frac{j}{\omega} \right) \parallel \left( -\frac{j}{\omega} \right)\] Simplifying the parallel reactive combination: \[\left( j4\omega - \frac{j}{\omega} \right) \parallel \left( -\frac{j}{\omega} \right) = \frac{\left( j4\omega - \frac{j}{\omega} \right) \left( -\frac{j}{\omega} \right)}{\left( j4\omega - \frac{j}{\omega} \right) + \left( -\frac{j}{\omega} \right)}\] Evaluating the numerator product: \[\left( j4\omega - \frac{j}{\omega} \right) \left( -\frac{j}{\omega} \right) = \frac{4\omega}{\omega} - \frac{1}{\omega^{2}} = 4 - \frac{1}{\omega^{2}}\] Evaluating the denominator sum: \[j4\omega - \frac{j}{\omega} - \frac{j}{\omega} = j\left( 4\omega - \frac{2}{\omega} \right)\] Substituting these components back into the parallel impedance equation yields: \[Z = 10 + \frac{4 - \frac{1}{\omega^{2}}}{j\left( 4\omega - \frac{2}{\omega} \right)}\] Bringing the complex imaginary unit \(j\) from the denominator to the numerator changes its sign: \[Z = 10 - j\left[ \frac{4 - \frac{1}{\omega^{2}}}{4\omega - \frac{2}{\omega}} \right]\] For the circuit to be operating at electrical resonance, the net reactive component or the imaginary part of the total network impedance \(Z\) must be identically equal to zero: \[\text{Im}(Z) = 0\] Setting the numerator of the imaginary term equal to zero: \[4 - \frac{1}{\omega_{\text{res}}^{2}} = 0\] \[\frac{1}{\omega_{\text{res}}^{2}} = 4\] \[\omega_{\text{res}}^{2} = \frac{1}{4} = 0.25 \implies \omega_{\text{res}} = 0.5\,\text{rad/sec}\] \[\boxed{(b)0.5rad/s}\]

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: \(s(t)\) is step response and \(h(t)\) is impulse response of a system. Its response \(y(t)\) for any input \(u(t)\) is given by
questions.explanation:
Let \(h(t)\) be the impulse response and \(s(t)\) be the step response of the system. Since \[s(t)=h(t)*u(t),\] the impulse response is \[h(t)=\frac{ds(t)}{dt}.\] For any input \(u(t)\), the output is \[y(t)=h(t)*u(t).\] Substituting \(h(t)=\dfrac{ds(t)}{dt}\), \[y(t)=\frac{ds(t)}{dt}*u(t).\] Using the differentiation property of convolution, \[\frac{ds(t)}{dt}*u(t)
=\frac{d}{dt}\left[s(t)*u(t)\right].\] Since \[s(t)*u(t)
=\int_{0}^{t}s(t-\tau)u(\tau)\,d\tau,\] we obtain \[y(t)
=\frac{d}{dt}\left[\int_{0}^{t}s(t-\tau)u(\tau)\,d\tau\right].\] \[\boxed{\text{(a) }\frac{d}{dt}\left[\int_{0}^{t}s(t-\tau)u(\tau)\,d\tau\right]}\]

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: A 10,bit A/D converter is used to digitize an analog signal in the 0 to 5,V range. The maximum peak to peak ripple voltage that can be allowed in the dc supply voltage is
questions.explanation:
Given:
  • Number of bits: \(n = 10\)
  • Input voltage range: \(V_{min} = 0\,\text{V}\) to \(V_{max} = 5\,\text{V}\)
1. Resolution and LSB Calculation:
The resolution of the ADC represents the smallest analog voltage change corresponding to a change of 1 Least Significant Bit (LSB) in the digital output code: \[\text{LSB} = \frac{V_{max} - V_{min}}{2^n} = \frac{5 - 0}{2^{10}} = \frac{5}{1024} \approx 0.00488\,\text{V} \approx 4.88\,\text{mV}\] Note: If the peak-to-peak power supply ripple voltage exceeds approximately one LSB (\(\approx 5\,\text{mV}\)), the internal reference references or comparison levels will fluctuate significantly. This variation can cause the digital output code to toggle or drift by one or more counts even when the actual analog input signal remains perfectly constant. Therefore, to prevent spurious fluctuations and maintain a stable conversion, the maximum allowable peak-to-peak ripple voltage must be restricted to approximately equal to one LSB, which is about \(5\,\text{mV}\). (D) Nearly 5 mV
Key points
  • The resolution of an ADC represents the smallest analog change that produces a change in digital output.
  • Any supply ripple exceeding the resolution will cause the ADC output to fluctuate by at least 1 LSB, introducing errors.
  • For high-precision design purposes, supply ripple should be kept well below 1 LSB (ideally \(\le 0.5\) LSB) to preserve accuracy.

A \(300\,\mathrm{kVA}\) transformer has \(95\%\) efficiency at full load \(0.8\,\mathrm{pf}\) lagging and \(96\%\) efficiency at half load, unity pf. The iron loss \((P_i)\) and copper loss \((P_c)\) in \(\mathrm{kW}\), under full load operation are

A \(220/440\,\mathrm{V}\), \(50\,\mathrm{Hz}\), \(5\,\mathrm{kVA}\) single phase transformer operates on \(220\,\mathrm{V},40\,\mathrm{Hz}\) supply with secondary winding. Then
options: the eddy current loss and hysteresis loss of the transformer decrease
the eddy current loss and hysteresis loss of the transformer increase
the hysteresis loss of the transformer increases while eddy current loss remains the same
the hysteresis loss remains the same whereas eddy current loss decreases
questions.explanation: Hysteresis loss is given by: \[P_{h}\propto B_{m}^{n}f\] Taking Steinmetz coefficient, \[n=2\] Since, \[V\propto B_{m}f\] Therefore, \[B_{m}\propto \frac{V}{f}\] Substituting in hysteresis loss expression: \[P_{h}\propto \left(\frac{V}{f}\right)^2f\] \[P_{h}\propto \frac{V^2}{f}\] For eddy current loss, \[P_{e}\propto B_{m}^{2}f^{2}\] Substituting, \[P_{e}\propto \left(\frac{V}{f}\right)^2f^{2}\] \[P_{e}\propto V^{2}\] Since applied voltage remains constant, eddy current loss remains constant. However, as frequency decreases, \[P_{h}\propto \frac{1}{f}\] Hence hysteresis loss increases. \[\boxed{C}\]

questions.subject: electrical-machines
questions.question:
Statement for Linked Questions Q3.08.1 and Q3.08.2:
A \(240\,\text{V}\), dc shunt motor draws \(15\,\text{A}\) while supplying the rated load at a speed of \(80\,\text{rad/s}\). The armature resistance is \(0.5\,\Omega\) and the field winding resistance is \(80\,\Omega\).

A cumulative compounded long shunt motor is driving a load at rated torque and rated speed. If the series field is shunted by a resistance equal to the resistance of the series field, keeping the torque constant., [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
[figure unavailable] If the series field is shunted by a resistance, then the current through the series field decreases. Hence, the series-field flux \(\phi_{se}\) decreases and the resultant flux becomes \[\phi_{\text{net}}=\phi_{sh}+\phi_{se}\] Since \(\phi_{se}\) is reduced, \[\phi_{\text{net,new}} < \phi_{\text{net,old}}\] For a DC motor, \[T \propto \phi I_{a}\] Assuming the load torque remains constant, \[T=\text{constant}\] Therefore, \[\phi_{\text{net}} I_{a} = \text{constant}\] When \(\phi_{\text{net}}\) decreases, the armature current must increase to maintain the same torque. \[I_{a,\text{new}} > I_{a,\text{old}}\] Hence, shunting the series field causes the armature current to increase. \[\boxed{A}\]
Key points
  • In a cumulative compound motor, resultant flux is \(\phi_{\text{net}}=\phi_{sh}+\phi_{se}\).
  • A diverter (shunt resistance) across the series field reduces series-field current.
  • Reduction in series-field current reduces series-field flux.
  • For constant load torque, \(T\propto \phi I_{a}\); therefore, a reduction in flux causes an increase in armature current.

Statement for Linked Questions (Q4.07.3,Q4.07.4 and Q4.07.5):
A three phase squirrel cage induction motor has a starting current of seven times the full load current and full load slip of \(5\%\).

A three phase slip ring induction motor is fed from the rotor side with stator winding short circuited. The frequency of the currents flowing in the short circuited stator is
questions.explanation: This is the case of an inverted induction motor, where the three-phase supply is applied to the rotor terminals and the stator winding is short-circuited. A rotating magnetic field is produced, which rotates at synchronous speed with respect to the rotor. This rotating field cuts the stator conductors and induces an emf in the short-circuited stator winding, causing current to flow. To reduce the relative speed between the magnetic field and the stator conductors, the rotor rotates in the same direction as the rotating field. Consequently, the relative speed reduces to the slip speed. Hence, the frequency of the emf induced in the stator is equal to the slip frequency. \[f_s = s f\] Therefore, the correct option is \[\boxed{A}\]

questions.subject: electrical-machines
questions.question:
Statement for Linked Questions (Q5.05.2 and Q5.05.3):
Statement for Linked Answer Questions 83a & 83b: A \(1000\,\text{kVA}\), \(6.6\,\text{kV}\), \(3\)-phase star connected cylindrical pole synchronous generator has a synchronous reactance of \(20\,\Omega\). Neglect the armature resistance and consider operation at full load and unity power factor.

A three phase alternator has negligible stator resistance. A short circuit test is conducted on this alternator. At a particular speed a field current of \(I_{f1}\) is required to drive the rated armature current. If the speed of the alternator is reduced to half, the field current required to maintain rated armature current
options: cannot be predicted due to insufficient data
questions.explanation:
For a short-circuit test on an alternator with negligible armature resistance, \[I_{sc}=\frac{E_{g}}{\sqrt{R_{a}^{2}+X_{s}^{2}}} \approx \frac{E_{g}}{X_{s}}\] The generated emf is proportional to speed and field flux: \[E_{g}\propto N\phi\] Assuming operation in the unsaturated region, \[\phi \propto I_{f}\] Hence, \[E_{g}\propto N I_{f}\] Also, synchronous reactance is \[X_{s}=2\pi f L_{s}\] Since frequency is proportional to speed, \[X_{s}\propto f \propto N\] Substituting in the short-circuit current expression, \[I_{sc}\propto \frac{N I_{f}}{N}\] \[I_{sc}\propto I_{f}\] Thus, the short-circuit current is independent of speed and depends only on the field current. Therefore, when the speed is reduced to half, the field current required to maintain the rated armature current remains unchanged. \[I_{f}=I_{f1}\] Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\text{ A}}\]
Key points
  • During short-circuit test, \(R_{a}\) is negligible compared to \(X_{s}\).
  • Generated emf: \[E_{g}\propto N\phi \propto N I_{f}\]
  • Synchronous reactance: \[X_{s}\propto N\]
  • Therefore, \[I_{sc}\propto \frac{N I_{f}}{N}=I_{f}\]
  • Short-circuit characteristic (SCC) is independent of speed.

Statement for Linked Answer Questions 83a & 83b: A \(1000\,\text{kVA}\), \(6.6\,\text{kV}\), \(3\)-phase star connected cylindrical pole synchronous generator has a synchronous reactance of \(20\,\Omega\). Neglect the armature resistance and consider operation at full load and unity power factor.

A synchronous motor operates at \(0.8\) p.f. lagging. If the field current of the motor is continuously increased
options: the power factor decreases upto a certain value of field current and thereafter it increases
the armature current increases upto a certain value of field current and thereafter it decreases
the power factor increases upto a certain value of field current and thereafter it decreases
the armature current decreases upto a certain value of field current and thereafter it increases
questions.explanation: A synchronous motor working at \(0.8\) lagging power factor is under-excited. If the excitation or field current is increased, the reactive power drawn from the AC supply decreases. Hence, the power factor tends to become unity. At unity power factor, the armature current becomes minimum. If the field current is increased further, the motor becomes over-excited and starts operating at leading power factor. The armature current again increases. Thus, the magnitude of armature current first decreases, reaches a minimum at unity power factor, and then increases. This is represented by the V-curve. \[\boxed{\text{C}}\]

questions.subject: power-systems
questions.question:
Answer the questions Q\(3.06.1\) and Q\(3.06.2\) based on the data below A generator feeds power to an infinite bus through a double circuit transmission line. A Three-phase fault occurs at the middle point of one of the lines. The infinite bus voltage is \(1\) pu, the transient internal voltage of the generator is \(1.1\) pu and the equivalent transfer admittance during fault is \(0.8\) pu. The \(100\) MVA generator has an inertia constant of \(5\) MJ/MVA and was delivering \(1.0\) pu power prior to the fault with rotor power angle of \(30^\circ\). The system frequency is \(50\) Hz.

The transient stability of the power system can be effectively improved by
questions.explanation:
Transient stability refers to the ability of a power system to remain in synchronism following a large disturbance such as:
  • Three-phase faults,
  • Single line-to-ground faults,
  • Sudden loss of generation,
  • Sudden switching of transmission lines.
The objective is to reduce the accelerating energy of the generator rotor during the fault and increase the decelerating energy after fault clearing. Let us examine each option. --- Option (A): Excitation control
Fast excitation systems improve voltage regulation and steady-state stability. Although they provide some improvement in transient stability, they are not the most effective method among the given options. Hence, Option (A) is not the best answer. --- Option (B): Phase shifting transformer
A phase-shifting transformer controls real power flow between transmission lines by introducing a phase-angle shift. It is primarily used for load flow control and congestion management rather than improving transient stability. Hence, Option (B) is incorrect. --- Option (C): Single pole switching circuit breakers
Most faults occurring on EHV transmission lines are single line-to-ground (SLG) faults. With conventional three-pole tripping, all three phases are disconnected during the fault, causing the electrical power output of the generator to become nearly zero. From the swing equation, \[P_a=P_m-P_e\] where
  • \(P_m\) = Mechanical input power,
  • \(P_e\) = Electrical output power,
  • \(P_a\) = Accelerating power.
If all three phases are opened, \[P_e\approx0\] therefore, \[P_a\approx P_m\] which produces maximum rotor acceleration. However, in single-pole switching, only the faulty phase is isolated while the two healthy phases continue to transmit power. Thus, \[P_e>0\] during the fault. Consequently, \[P_a=P_m-P_e\] is significantly reduced, thereby reducing rotor acceleration and improving transient stability. This increases the critical clearing time and the stability margin of the system. Hence, Option (C) is correct. --- Option (D): Increasing the turbine valve opening
Increasing turbine valve opening increases the mechanical input power, \[P_m\] which increases accelerating power during a fault. This adversely affects transient stability. Hence, Option (D) is incorrect. --- Therefore, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\text{(C) Single pole switching circuit breakers}}\]

questions.subject: power-systems
questions.ref: Power System Matrices and Load Flow Q1
options: Constant current drawn from the bus
Constant impedance connected at the bus
Voltage and frequency dependent source at the bus
Constant real and reactive power drawn from the bus
questions.explanation:
Load flow (power flow) analysis is used to determine the steady-state operating condition of a power system. The unknown quantities generally computed are:
  • Bus voltage magnitudes,
  • Bus voltage phase angles,
  • Active power flow,
  • Reactive power flow,
  • Transmission losses.
To solve the power flow equations, each bus is modeled according to the quantities specified and the quantities to be determined. The common bus types are:
  • Slack (Swing) Bus
  • PV (Generator) Bus
  • PQ (Load) Bus
--- Load (PQ) Bus Representation
At a load bus, the connected load is assumed to consume specified amounts of active and reactive power. Therefore, \[P=P_L=\text{constant}\] and \[Q=Q_L=\text{constant}\] These specified values are independent of the unknown bus voltage during the iterative solution of the load-flow problem. The quantities computed during the load-flow iterations are \[|V|\] and \[\delta\] Thus, a load bus is modeled as a constant real and reactive power demand. --- Discussion of Options
Option (A): Constant current drawn from the bus This model is sometimes used for specific load studies but is not the standard assumption in conventional power-flow analysis. Hence, Option (A) is incorrect. --- Option (B): Constant impedance connected at the bus A constant impedance model causes the load power to vary with the square of the bus voltage. Although such models exist, they are not the standard representation used in classical load-flow analysis. Hence, Option (B) is incorrect. --- Option (C): Voltage and frequency dependent source at the bus Loads are modeled as power-consuming elements, not as sources. Hence, Option (C) is incorrect. --- Option (D): Constant real and reactive power drawn from the bus This is the standard PQ bus model used in conventional load-flow analysis. Hence, Option (D) is correct. Therefore, \[\boxed{\text{(D) Constant real and reactive power drawn from the bus}}\]

questions.subject: power-systems
questions.question: The distribution system shown in the figure is to be protected by an overcurrent system of protection. For proper fault discrimination, directional overcurrent relays will be required at locations
questions.explanation:
An overcurrent relay operates whenever the current exceeds a predetermined pickup value. However, in an interconnected power system supplied from more than one source, fault current can flow in either direction depending on the fault location. In such systems, ordinary non-directional overcurrent relays cannot always discriminate between forward and reverse faults. Therefore, directional overcurrent relays are installed wherever bidirectional fault current is possible. --- Relay at Location 1 Relay 1 is located adjacent to the left-hand source. Since the source can supply fault current only towards the feeder, the current direction is always known. Hence, a non-directional overcurrent relay is sufficient. --- Relay at Location 4 Similarly, Relay 4 is adjacent to the right-hand source. Fault current always flows away from the source towards the network. Therefore, a non-directional relay is adequate. --- Relay at Location 5 Relay 5 protects the load feeder. The connected load cannot feed current back into the system because it is not a generating source. Consequently, fault current through Relay 5 always flows in one direction only. Thus, Relay 5 also need not be directional. --- Relay at Location 2 Relay 2 lies between two power sources. Consider a fault between Relays 1 and 2. The left source feeds the fault towards the left, whereas the right source feeds the fault towards the left through Relay 2. Now consider a fault between Relays 2 and 3. The direction of current through Relay 2 reverses compared with the previous case. Therefore, Relay 2 experiences bidirectional fault current and must be directional. --- Relay at Location 3 Similarly, Relay 3 is located between two power sources. Depending on whether the fault occurs on the left or the right side, the current through Relay 3 changes direction. Hence, Relay 3 must also be a directional overcurrent relay. --- Discussion of Options
Option (A): 1 and 4 Incorrect. Relays 1 and 4 are adjacent to source buses where current direction is fixed. --- Option (B): 2 and 3 Correct. Only these relays experience reversal of fault current direction. --- Option (C): 1, 4 and 5 Incorrect. Relay 5 protects a load feeder and does not require directional discrimination. --- Option (D): 2, 3 and 5 Incorrect. Relay 5 carries fault current in only one direction because the load cannot contribute fault current. --- Therefore, \[\boxed{\text{(B) Relays at locations 2 and 3}}\]
Key points
  • Directional overcurrent relays are required wherever fault current may flow in either direction.
  • Source-end relays usually do not require directional elements.
  • Load feeders supplied from one direction generally use non-directional overcurrent relays.
  • Interconnected and ring-main systems commonly require directional protection.

A voltage commutated chopper operating at \(1\text{ kHz}\) is used to control the speed of dc motor as shown in figure. The load current is assumed to be constant at \(10\text{ A}\) [figure unavailable]

A chopper operating at a fixed frequency is feeding an R-L load. As the duty ratio of the chopper is increased from \(25\%\) to \(75\%\), the ripple in the load current
options: Decreases, reaches a minimum at \(50\%\) duty ratio and then increases
Increases, reaches a maximum at \(50\%\) duty ratio and then decreases
Keeps on increasing as the duty ratio is increased
questions.explanation: The ripple in the load current of a chopper-fed \(R\!-\!L\) load is given by \[\Delta I_L = \frac{V_s\,\alpha(1-\alpha)}{fL}\] where, \[\alpha=\text{Duty cycle}\] Since \[\Delta I_L \propto \alpha(1-\alpha),\] the maximum ripple occurs when \[\frac{d}{d\alpha}\left[\alpha(1-\alpha)\right]=0\] \[1-2\alpha=0\] \[\Rightarrow \alpha=0.5\] [figure unavailable] Thus, as the duty cycle increases from \(25\%\) to \(50\%\), the ripple increases. Beyond \(50\%\), the ripple decreases. Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{(C) \ \text{Increases, reaches a maximum at 50\% duty ratio and then decreases}}\]
